2049	[00:23:31] Kerem Yalçın: Uh. Good question. If they're complaining, it's the complaint branch. If they just ask something unrelated, the out-of-scope question.
2050	[00:23:38] Selin Aydın: And if they explicitly want an agent, agent. Without trying to convince them.
2051	[00:23:42] Ozan Er: Okay, that's clear enough for us.
2052	[00:23:45] Kerem Yalçın: Guys, I have a hard stop at three, so let's do a quick recap? Deniz?
2053	[00:23:50] Deniz Arı: Sure, quickly, and I'll send it in writing too.
2054	[00:23:53] Deniz Arı: Silence: first two times, short repeat of the question. Third time "Sesinizi alamadığım için görüşmeyi sonlandırıyorum." and the call is closed.
2055	[00:24:02] Deniz Arı: Unclear answer or refusal: ask again, three tries per question. After three: "Size şu anda yardımcı olamıyorum. Sizi ana menüye aktarıyorum." Repeating information doesn't count.
2056	[00:24:12] Deniz Arı: Non-Turkish: "Sizi ana menüye aktarıyorum."
2057	[00:24:15] Deniz Arı: Out of scope: "Size bu konuda yardımcı olamıyorum. Sizi ana menüye aktarmamı ister misiniz?" Yes, main menu. Continue, back to the flow. Unclear, ask again, three tries.
2058	[00:24:26] Deniz Arı: Card selection: same name, last four. Same last four: "Son dört hanesi 4253 olan birden fazla kartınız var. Kartınızın son altı hanesini söyler misiniz?" Same last six: "Son altı hanesi aynı olan birden fazla kartınız var. Kart numaranızı söyler misiniz?"
2059	[00:24:42] Selin Aydın: With the real digits, not 4253.
2060	[00:24:44] Deniz Arı: Yes, of course, from the service.
2061	[00:24:46] Deniz Arı: Angry customer: up to three calming replies, then "Sizi müşteri temsilcimize aktarıyorum." No reaction to insults.
2062	[00:24:53] Deniz Arı: Currency names always in full, Türk Lirası, Dolar, Euro, İngiliz Sterlini, also in the no-debt sentence.
2063	[00:25:00] Deniz Arı: Statement week: once per calendar year. Not offered if the right is used. Mentioning the limit is optional. Kerem checks the pre-check service with Mert.
2064	[00:25:09] Deniz Arı: Joint statement: before the confirm question, "Bu değişiklik kartınıza bağlı [bağlı kart adı] kartınızı da etkileyecek." For the linked card holder, before the confirm question, that the main card is affected too.
2065	[00:25:21] Deniz Arı: Normal end, nothing else wanted: "Sizi ana menüye yönlendiriyorum." for now, to look at again with the routing project.
2066	[00:25:28] Elçin Ural: One correction. For the joint statement, not only "before confirming". Before the question. I want the customer to hear it, and then the question comes.
2067	[00:25:35] Deniz Arı: Yes, that's what I meant. Sentence first, then "Onaylıyor musunuz?".
2068	[00:25:39] Elçin Ural: Okay.
2069	[00:25:40] Kerem Yalçın: Good. Selin, you'll fix the document?
2070	[00:25:43] Selin Aydın: I'll fix what I can by tomorrow. The edge case section I'll redo anyway, it's a mess.
2071	[00:25:51] Deniz Arı: I'll send it, maybe not today, tomorrow or Friday.
2072	[00:25:54] Selin Aydın: Fine.
2073	[00:25:55] Burcu Tan: And I'll send the silence timing from the IVR. And I'll fix my prompts for the yearly limit, but that's for the IVR, not for you.
2074	[00:26:02] Ozan Er: Thanks Burcu.
2075	[00:26:04] Kerem Yalçın: Anything else? The [inaudible] mobile app topic we do next week, not today.
2076	[00:26:09] Selin Aydın: Next week, yes. Ah, and Elçin, mandatory texts, is there anything the assistant must say at the start?
2077	[00:26:15] Elçin Ural: I'm checking. I'll write to you. I don't think so for this flow because the customer is already identified in the IVR, but let me confirm.
2078	[00:26:22] Selin Aydın: Okay, thanks.
2079	[00:26:24] Deniz Arı: One more for us, sorry, thirty seconds. When the debt service doesn't answer, an error, we go to an agent, not main menu. Still okay?
2080	[00:26:31] Kerem Yalçın: Yes. Service error, agent. The customer did nothing wrong, they shouldn't land in the menu.
2081	[00:26:36] Deniz Arı: And the sentence from the mails stays, "Şu anda işleminizi gerçekleştiremiyorum, sizi müşteri temsilcimize aktarıyorum."
2082	[00:26:42] Kerem Yalçın: Yes.
2083	[00:26:43] Deniz Arı: Perfect, that's all from us.
2084	[00:26:45] Ozan Er: Oh, last thing, the digits. When the customer says "kırk iki elli üç" for the last four, that's the same as "dört iki beş üç", we just map it, we don't read it back.
2085	[00:26:53] Selin Aydın: Yes, any way they say it.
2086	[00:26:55] Kerem Yalçın: Okay, I really have to go. Thanks everyone, good session.
2087	[00:26:58] Burcu Tan: Bye bye.
2088	[00:26:59] Elçin Ural: Thanks, bye.
2089	[00:27:00] Selin Aydın: Bye. Deniz, Ozan, can you stay one minute?
2090	[00:27:03] Deniz Arı: Sure.
2091	[00:27:05] Selin Aydın: Is it okay for you if the document only catches up next week? I have the quarterly report this week and honestly...
2092	[00:27:11] Deniz Arı: No problem. We have our notes from today.
2093	[00:27:15] Selin Aydın: Thanks. And the six-digit comment, you'll put it?
2094	[00:27:18] Deniz Arı: Yes, right after this.
2095	[00:27:20] Ozan Er: Selin, one question about the test cards, the two Yıldız cards in the test data, do they really share the last four?
2096	[00:27:26] Selin Aydın: I think so, Mert built them for exactly that. Ask him, I'm not a hundred percent sure.
2097	[00:27:31] Ozan Er: Okay, I'll ask.
2098	[00:27:32] Selin Aydın: Okay. Thanks both. Talk Friday.

Statement debt analysis session - Freya Bank / Freya
Wednesday 7 October 2026, 14:30, video call
Recording: automatic transcript, excerpt. Speaker detection may be wrong where people talk over each other.
Participants: Selin Aydın, Kerem Yalçın, Burcu Tan, Elçin Ural (joined at about 00:14), Deniz Arı, Ozan Er

[...]

[00:01:12] Selin Aydın: ...okay, I think it's recording now. Kerem is in another call, he said five minutes.
[00:01:17] Burcu Tan: Then it's ten minutes [laughs].
[00:01:19] Selin Aydın: [laughs] Probably. Deniz, Ozan, can you hear me fine?
[00:01:22] Deniz Arı: Yes. Hi Selin, hi Burcu.
[00:01:24] Ozan Er: Hi. Sorry, my camera is off, the internet here is a bit weak today.
[00:01:28] Burcu Tan: Are you at the office?
[00:01:29] Ozan Er: No, at home, the building is doing something with the cables. Since Monday.
[00:01:33] Burcu Tan: Ours was like that last year, three weeks. Good luck.
[00:01:36] Selin Aydın: Okay. While we wait for Kerem, maybe two small things on the reading part? Those don't need him.
[00:01:42] Deniz Arı: Sure. We had a few small ones too.
[00:01:45] Selin Aydın: First, the order. When a card has debt in more than one currency. I wrote Türk Lirası first, then the foreign currencies. Is that clear enough in the document?
[00:01:54] Ozan Er: Mostly. We read it as: the card intro with the statement date, then Türk Lirası, then Dolar, Euro, İngiliz Sterlini in that order, then one sentence for all the currencies with no debt, then the due date.
[00:02:06] Selin Aydın: Yes, exactly that.
[00:02:08] Ozan Er: And the remaining automatic payment, if there is one, before the due date.
[00:02:12] Selin Aydın: Yes. Before the due date.
[00:02:14] Burcu Tan: The IVR reads the due date last too. People remember the last thing they hear.
[00:02:18] Deniz Arı: Makes sense.
[00:02:20] Ozan Er: Then for the due date the sentence is "Borçlarınız için son ödeme tarihiniz [son ödeme tarihi]'dir." with the date like "21 Ekim 2025". Day, month name, year.
[00:02:30] Selin Aydın: Yes. And if the due date is today, it should say today. Not the date.
[00:02:35] Ozan Er: "Borçlarınız için son ödeme tarihiniz bugündür." Okay, we have that.
[00:02:39] Selin Aydın: Good.
[00:02:41] Deniz Arı: Second small one from us. After the debt is read, if the customer has more than one card, what comes first, the other-card question or the offer? E-mail and the week change.
[00:02:51] Selin Aydın: Hm. I'd say other card first. The customer called for the debt. If they have another card, maybe they want that one too.
[00:02:58] Deniz Arı: So: "Başka bir kartınızın borcunu öğrenmek ister misiniz?" and only when the cards are done, or they say no, the offer.
[00:03:05] Selin Aydın: Yes. Let's confirm with Kerem but I think he'll agree.
[00:03:09] Burcu Tan: And if they have only one card, you don't ask the other-card question, obviously.
[00:03:13] Deniz Arı: No, then straight to the offer.
[00:03:15] Ozan Er: And the offer only has what the customer can actually do. That's why we keep asking about the e-mail and the yearly right, it's connected.
[00:03:21] Selin Aydın: Yes, we'll get to that, it's in the yellow list.
[00:03:24] Ozan Er: Okay.
[00:03:26] Deniz Arı: The amounts, that's clear, I think. Lira and kuruş in full, like "bin iki yüz lira elli kuruş", and if kuruş is zero we don't say "sıfır kuruş".
[00:03:35] Selin Aydın: Yes. And the foreign currencies with cents. Sterlin with pence, um, "peni".
[00:03:40] Ozan Er: Yes, we did that already.
[00:03:42] Burcu Tan: Can I ask something off topic, sorry. Selin, the training on Thursday, is it still on?
[00:03:47] Selin Aydın: Which one? The onboarding group?
[00:03:49] Burcu Tan: The onboarding group, yes. I have two people starting.
[00:03:52] Selin Aydın: I think so. I'll check and write you.
[00:03:54] Burcu Tan: Thanks.
[00:03:56] Ozan Er: One more on the card question. The example card names in "Hangi kartınızın borcunu öğrenmek istersiniz? Örneğin, [kart adı] veya [kart adı] diyebilirsiniz." Those are the customer's own cards, max two, right?
[00:04:07] Selin Aydın: Yes. Never a card the customer doesn't have. It would confuse them.
[00:04:11] Ozan Er: Okay.
[00:04:12] Deniz Arı: And after the customer picks the card, we go to the debt. No "okay, continuing with your Yıldız card" sentence.
[00:04:18] Selin Aydın: No, that's not needed. The card name is in the first sentence of the reading anyway.
[00:04:23] Deniz Arı: Exactly.
[00:04:24] Selin Aydın: Okay. Let me open the edge cases, so we're ready when Kerem joins. Let me just... the sharing is not... one second.
[00:04:31] Burcu Tan: We see your mail.
[00:04:33] Selin Aydın: Oops. Okay. Now?
[00:04:35] Burcu Tan: Now a white page.
[00:04:37] Selin Aydın: It's loading. The file is big.
[00:04:40] Ozan Er: [inaudible] ...every time.
[00:04:43] Selin Aydın: Sorry?
[00:04:44] Ozan Er: Nothing, I said the same happens to me every time with that tool.
[00:04:48] Selin Aydın: [laughs] Okay. I'll stop sharing until Kerem is in.

[...]

[00:06:41] Kerem Yalçın: ...no, it's fine, the other meeting ran late, sorry. Can everyone hear me?
[00:06:44] Deniz Arı: Yes, loud and clear.
[00:06:45] Burcu Tan: You're a bit echoey Kerem.
[00:06:47] Kerem Yalçın: Hm. Better? I switched to the headset.
[00:06:49] Burcu Tan: Better, yes.
[00:06:51] Selin Aydın: Okay so, um, I'll share my screen. Can you see the document? The statement debt one, the September analysis.
[00:06:58] Ozan Er: Yes, we see it.
[00:07:00] Selin Aydın: Good. So I put the open points in yellow, there are, let me count, eleven? Twelve. We don't have to do all of them today but the edge cases I really want to close because Deniz's team is already building.
[00:07:13] Deniz Arı: Yes, that would help a lot. Most of our questions are in the edge case part anyway. The happy path is quite clear.
[00:07:20] Selin Aydın: Okay. Then let's start with, um, silence. Because that one I wrote quickly and I'm not happy with it.
[00:07:27] Selin Aydın: Right now it says if the customer is silent three times, we go to the main menu.
[00:07:32] Kerem Yalçın: That's what we agreed in September, no?
[00:07:34] Selin Aydın: That's what I wrote, yes.
[00:07:36] Kerem Yalçın: I think it's fine. Main menu, they can choose something else there.
[00:07:40] Ozan Er: Can I ask one thing about the first two? What does the assistant do on the first silence? Because the document only talks about the third.
[00:07:47] Selin Aydın: Ah. Good point. It repeats the question, I'd say.
[00:07:50] Ozan Er: The whole question or a short version?
[00:07:53] Selin Aydın: Short. Like, it asked which card, the customer says nothing, it asks again shorter. Not the whole sentence with the examples.
[00:08:00] Ozan Er: Okay, so silence one, short repeat. Silence two, short repeat. Silence three...
[00:08:05] Kerem Yalçın: Main menu. Let's keep it, we can come back if Burcu has something.
[00:08:09] Burcu Tan: I have something but let me check it first, I'm not sure what the IVR does today exactly. I'll look while you continue.
[00:08:15] Kerem Yalçın: Okay.
[00:08:17] Selin Aydın: Next one. Unclear answer. Or the customer refuses to give the information, like we ask the last four digits and they say "why do you need it", that kind of thing.
[00:08:26] Deniz Arı: For us these are the same branch. The question is asked again and the customer gets three tries. After three, main menu. Is that okay?
[00:08:33] Selin Aydın: Three tries per question, yes. That matches what we do in the IVR.
[00:08:37] Burcu Tan: Yes, three. [inaudible] ...the IVR also counts per menu, not per call.
[00:08:42] Ozan Er: Per question then. And if the customer just asks to hear it again, like "can you repeat the amount", that doesn't count as a try, right?
[00:08:49] Selin Aydın: No, no. Repeating is not a failure. They can ask as many times as they want.
[00:08:53] Ozan Er: Okay. And what does it say when the three tries are gone? Because in the document there's, um, there's a sentence at the bottom of the exit table.
[00:09:00] Selin Aydın: Yes, I wrote "Sizi ana menüye yönlendiriyorum."
[00:09:04] Burcu Tan: The IVR says "aktarıyorum". Not "yönlendiriyorum". We had a whole discussion about that two years ago, I don't want to start it again [laughs].
[00:09:11] Kerem Yalçın: And I think it should say why. Not just "I'm transferring you". The customer tried three times, they should hear that we can't help right now.
[00:09:18] Deniz Arı: So something like "Size şu anda yardımcı olamıyorum" and then the transfer?
[00:09:22] Kerem Yalçın: Yes. Selin, can you write it full?
[00:09:25] Selin Aydın: Typing. "Size şu anda yardımcı olamıyorum. Sizi ana menüye aktarıyorum." Two sentences.
[00:09:31] Burcu Tan: That's good. That's close to the IVR line.
[00:09:33] Ozan Er: And for the normal end, when the customer says "no, nothing else, thanks"? Same sentence?
[00:09:38] Kerem Yalçın: No, there nothing went wrong. There it's just the transfer.
[00:09:42] Selin Aydın: For the normal end I'd keep "Sizi ana menüye yönlendiriyorum." for now. When the call routing project comes we look at all these sentences together anyway.
[00:09:50] Burcu Tan: Fine for me, as long as the failure one says "aktarıyorum".
[00:09:53] Deniz Arı: Noted. Failure after three tries: "Size şu anda yardımcı olamıyorum. Sizi ana menüye aktarıyorum." Normal end stays as it is in the document.
[00:10:01] Selin Aydın: Yes.
[00:10:03] Kerem Yalçın: Can someone close the door, there's a delivery guy shouting outside here.
[00:10:07] Burcu Tan: That's on your side Kerem [laughs].
[00:10:09] Kerem Yalçın: Ah, yes, sorry. One second. [inaudible]
[00:10:20] Kerem Yalçın: Okay. Go on.
[00:10:22] Selin Aydın: Non-Turkish. Customer speaks English or Arabic or German, whatever.
[00:10:27] Deniz Arı: We assume this flow answers only in Turkish?
[00:10:30] Kerem Yalçın: Yes. For now only Turkish. There is an English menu in the IVR, they can go from the main menu.
[00:10:36] Ozan Er: So it doesn't answer the question, it just transfers. What does it say? Turkish, I assume, since the call is Turkish.
[00:10:42] Burcu Tan: Just "Sizi ana menüye aktarıyorum." Nothing else. They won't understand a long sentence anyway.
[00:10:47] Selin Aydın: Okay. "Sizi ana menüye aktarıyorum." for non-Turkish. Writing.
[00:10:52] Deniz Arı: Good.
[00:10:54] Selin Aydın: Out of scope next. So in the document I wrote out of scope goes directly to the main menu.
[00:11:00] Deniz Arı: Yes, that's one we wanted to discuss. Ozan, you had the example from the tests.
[00:11:05] Ozan Er: Yes. So we tried it like that and the problem is, the customer asks something small, like, um, "what is my card limit" in the middle of the card selection, and boom, they're in the main menu. They didn't want to leave, they just asked something.
[00:11:18] Kerem Yalçın: Hm.
[00:11:19] Ozan Er: So our proposal: the assistant says it can't help with that, and asks if they want to go to the main menu. If yes, main menu. If they want to continue, back to where they were.
[00:11:28] Kerem Yalçın: I like that. Selin?
[00:11:30] Selin Aydın: Yes, I'm okay. What is the sentence exactly?
[00:11:33] Ozan Er: We had something like "Bu konuda size yardımcı olamıyorum, ana menüye..." uh, I don't remember our wording.
[00:11:39] Kerem Yalçın: Let's make it consistent with the one we just wrote. "Size şu anda yardımcı olamıyorum" style.
[00:11:45] Selin Aydın: So: "Size bu konuda yardımcı olamıyorum. Sizi ana menüye aktarmamı ister misiniz?"
[00:11:51] Burcu Tan: Yes, that sounds natural.
[00:11:53] Kerem Yalçın: Good. Keep it.
[00:11:55] Deniz Arı: And if the answer to that question is unclear? Like they say "hmm, well, I don't know"?
[00:12:00] Selin Aydın: Same as every other question. Ask again, three tries.
[00:12:04] Deniz Arı: And after three, the failure sentence and main menu.
[00:12:07] Selin Aydın: Yes.
[00:12:08] Ozan Er: Good, I'm writing it in our sheet. Out of scope: "Size bu konuda yardımcı olamıyorum. Sizi ana menüye aktarmamı ister misiniz?" Yes, main menu. Continue, back to flow. Unclear, ask again, three tries.
[00:12:20] Kerem Yalçın: Wait, payment is not out of scope in that sense. If someone wants to pay, that goes to an agent, we said it in the e-mails.
[00:12:27] Deniz Arı: Yes, yes, payment is separate. Payment and disputes go to an agent. This is only for things that have nothing to do with the statement.
[00:12:33] Kerem Yalçın: Okay. Just so it's clear.
[00:12:35] Selin Aydın: Next, the angry customer. In the document: one calming reply, then agent.
[00:12:41] Kerem Yalçın: Yes, that's fine I think. We don't want the bot arguing with an angry customer.
[00:12:46] Deniz Arı: Okay. One calming sentence and then "Sizi müşteri temsilcimize aktarıyorum."
[00:12:51] Ozan Er: And insults, we don't answer the insult itself, right? It just stays polite.
[00:12:55] Kerem Yalçın: Never answers the insult. Stays polite, yes.
[00:12:58] Selin Aydın: Okay, that one stays as written then.
[00:13:01] Selin Aydın: Card selection. This is the long one. Mert isn't here but I talked to him yesterday.
[00:13:07] Deniz Arı: Okay, go.
[00:13:09] Selin Aydın: So. The customer has two cards with the same name. Two Yıldız cards, for example. We ask the last four digits.
[00:13:17] Ozan Er: And the question is "Yıldız isimli birden fazla kartınız var. Kartınızın son dört hanesini söyler misiniz?" That one we have from your document, yes.
[00:13:24] Selin Aydın: Yes. Now, what if the last four are also the same? It's rare but it happens, with renewed cards, or, um, with some business customers.
[00:13:33] Kerem Yalçın: How rare?
[00:13:35] Selin Aydın: I don't have a number. Mert said it exists.
[00:13:38] Kerem Yalçın: Okay.
[00:13:39] Selin Aydın: In the document I wrote: if the last four are the same, ask the full card number.
[00:13:44] Deniz Arı: We'd prefer one step in between. Last six digits. Most people can read six digits off the card without trouble, the full number is sixteen digits, people make mistakes, and saying the full number on the phone, some customers don't like it.
[00:13:56] Elçin Ural: Sorry, I'm joining late. Hello everyone. What are we on?
[00:13:59] Selin Aydın: Hi Elçin. Card selection, two cards same last four digits.
[00:14:03] Elçin Ural: Ah okay. Go on, I'll catch up.
[00:14:05] Deniz Arı: So, last four, then last six, then only if the last six are also the same, the full card number.
[00:14:12] Elçin Ural: From my side it's better if we ask less of the number. Six instead of sixteen, yes, fine.
[00:14:17] Kerem Yalçın: Okay, I'm fine. Selin, sentences?
[00:14:20] Selin Aydın: Um. For the six. "Son dört hanesi 4253 olan birden fazla kartınız var. Kartınızın son altı hanesini söyler misiniz?" With the real four digits of course, I just put the ones from the test card.
[00:14:33] Ozan Er: Yes, the digits come from the service. And for the full number?
[00:14:37] Selin Aydın: "Son altı hanesi aynı olan birden fazla kartınız var. Kart numaranızı söyler misiniz?"
[00:14:43] Ozan Er: Okay. And the digits, when the assistant says "4253" it's digit by digit. Dört, iki, beş, üç. Not "kırk iki elli üç".
[00:14:51] Burcu Tan: Yes, the IVR also reads digit by digit.
[00:14:54] Elçin Ural: And it never reads the full number back. Even if the customer says it.
[00:14:58] Deniz Arı: Never. It doesn't repeat what the customer said either, it just goes to the debt of that card.
[00:15:03] Elçin Ural: Good.
[00:15:05] Selin Aydın: Okay. I'll ask Deniz to add the six-digit step as a comment in my document, I'll put it in properly later.
[00:15:11] Deniz Arı: Sure, I'll do it after the call.
[00:15:13] Burcu Tan: Can I go back to silence? I checked.
[00:15:16] Selin Aydın: Yes, go.
[00:15:17] Burcu Tan: So in the IVR today, after the third no-input, we don't send them to the main menu. We hang up. There's a sentence, then disconnect.
[00:15:25] Kerem Yalçın: Really? I thought it went back to the menu.
[00:15:28] Burcu Tan: Only in the main menu itself it loops once. In the sub-menus after three no-inputs, it's goodbye. The logic is, if we can't hear the customer three times, either the line is broken or they left the phone. Sending them to the menu is just more silence.
[00:15:42] Deniz Arı: That makes sense for us too. If there's nobody there, the main menu will also time out.
[00:15:47] Kerem Yalçın: Okay, then let's do the same. Hang up.
[00:15:50] Elçin Ural: The customer should hear why the call is ending. Not just click.

The full answers of every service for every customer are in `test-customers.json`. If you write a mock, serve exactly those bodies with exactly those status codes; this page is only the overview. ## How the JSON is laid out `customers` is the customer list. Each customer has `customerNo`, `firstName`, `lastName` and `services`. 1	# Freya platform knowledge for the builder
2	
3	Read this once, in full, before you write `build_agent.py`. It holds what is true for every brief: how the platform behaves, what our library does, and the shape that works. It holds no rule of any brief. The values in the examples are invented.
4	
5	The worked example is in `example/` next to this file: an invented brief, its tool API, `ledger.md`, `spec.json`, `build_agent.py` and `test_rules.py`. It passes every check. It shows how to load the spec, call the library, build the workflow and test the code. Its business, flow, prompts and lines are only an illustration: design your nodes from your ledger, and take every prompt, line and value from your brief.
6	
7	## 1. The library (`builder/blocks/`)
8	
9	Import it in `build_agent.py`. `PYTHONPATH` already points at the repository.
10	
11	| Module | Use |
12	|---|---|
13	| `tools.load_api(path)` | Reads the tool API file. Returns operation name (the route without its first `/`; any other `/` or `.` becomes `_`) → `url`, `method`, `fields` (name → schema), `parents`, `required`, `response`. OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2. A body wrapped in an envelope object (`{"data": {...}}`) is opened: `fields` are the leaf names, and `make_tool` puts them back in their objects. Bake and read leaf names only. |
14	| `tools.make_tool(api, name, baked=..., post_code=..., description=...)` | An `api_call` tool. `baked` maps a body field to a fixed value or a `"{{variable}}"` the workflow sets. Every other field is filled by the model (its type, description and enum come from the API file). `post_code` runs in the post-hook with `d` = the whole JSON body the API returned, envelope included: when the response schema in `tool_api.json` wraps the fields (`{"data": {...}, "result": {...}}`), read them by that path (`d['data']['status']`), never at the top level. `result` is the platform's wrapper, not the API body. Set `d['what_to_do_next']`. |
15	| `tools.field_values(api, name, field)` | The enum of a field, or `[]`. |
16	| `nodes.conversation / code_node / api_node / end_node / workflow` | Valid nodes. `code_node` wraps the code in `try`, writes the `fallbacks` and `<node>_code_error` on an exception, and refuses `{{` or `}}`. `workflow` refuses an unknown target or a duplicate name. |
17	| `nodes.cond / any_of / all_of / is_true / go / always / intent / field / tts` | Conditions, transitions, extraction fields, fixed lines. `is_true` tests `"true"` and `"True"`. |
18	| `patterns.start(next)` | The empty initial code node. Always use it (fact 3.6). |
19	| `patterns.close_tool(api, name, baked)` | The closing tool as an end-of-call tool. Put it in `workflow(..., tools=[...])`. Empty fields are not sent. |
20	| `patterns.close_sequence(name, values, goodbye)` | A code node that sets the closing variables, then an `end_call` node that says the goodbye. |
21	| `patterns.state_tool(name, description, params, body)` | A `code_exec` tool the model calls. The body reads the model's arguments from `params` and writes `vars`. |
22	| `patterns.record_with_retry(name, tool, attempts, ok_target, fail_target)` | An engine-run write: a reset code node and one `api_request` node per attempt. Bake every body field of `tool` from variables the code set. Route to `name` when the code says so. Use it for every write whose values the code decided. |
23	| `patterns.negotiation_tool(kinds, policy, list_var)` | The state tool of the negotiation node, with the engine built in: state per product, several answers in one call (`answers`), the model's one-sentence `reply` to a question, one line per turn, no line said twice, account order, the end. You write only the brief's policy for one product: `decide(it, kind, amount, day)` → the words to say, `first_ask(it)`, `finish(items, confirmed)` → one final read-back (`dict(say=...)`) when the brief wants all items read back together, or the write fields, or a close key. See the docstring and the example. |
24	| `patterns.negotiation_nodes(name, task, tools, statement, transitions, max_turns, max_turn_target)` | The negotiation node and its loop. The first entry speaks `statement`; after each tool call that chose a line, the code speaks the line with fixed text (`tts`), so the model cannot change an offer. Pass your routes (writes, transfer, closes) as `transitions`. Use it instead of a `conversation` node for the negotiation. |
25	| `patterns.write_loop(name, api, tool, fields, baked, attempts, done_target)` | Engine-run writes for a list of items, one call per item, each with `attempts` tries. The code puts `[{"fields": {...}, "status": "pending"}, ...]` as JSON in `vars['<name>_list']` and routes to `name`; each item ends `ok` or `failed`; then the call goes to `done_target`. Use it for one write per item. |
26	| `patterns.answer_tool(questions)` | The state tool for identity answers. The model reports the parts said in each message (day, month, year, digits, chars, text); kinds: `["date", 0]`, `["digits", n]`, `["alnum", n]` for a code of letters and digits with a known length (a postcode, a reference: upper case, no spaces, spoken digits and "double" read), `["text", 0]` for anything else; the code joins parts over turns and sets `id_send = "yes"`, `id_question`, `id_answer` when an answer is complete. It writes `id_guide` every turn. |
27	| `patterns.identity_check(name, verify_tool, back_node, routes, guide_code)` | The engine-run identity check: reset node, `api_request` node `<name>_check`, and a code node that runs `guide_code` with `r(field)` = the backend's result field, then the `routes` (passed, failed), else back to `back_node`. |
28	| `patterns.guard_hook(condition)` | A `pre_process_code` that makes the call fail when the condition is true, so the backend records nothing. The condition can read `vars` and `body` (the request body). |
29	| `coderun.with_dates(body)` | Puts the date helpers in front of a snippet: `is_business_day(d, holidays)`, `nth_business_day_after(d, n, holidays)` (counts from the day after `d`), `next_business_day_on_or_after`, `last_business_day_of_week` (Monday–Sunday week of `d`), `this_weekday(d, wd)`, `next_weekday(d, wd)` (0 = Monday). Also `date` and `timedelta`. |
30	| `coderun.node_code / tool_code / run_snippet / run_tool` | For `test_rules.py`: get a node's or a tool's code from the workflow and run it locally with `vars` (and `params`). |
31	| `coderun.run_post_hook(tool, body)` | For `test_rules.py`: run a tool's post-hook on a response body (envelope included) and get the `result` it wrote. |
32	
33	Commands (run them from the run folder):
34	
35	```
36	$BUILDER_PYTHON build_agent.py                                   # writes workflow.json
37	$BUILDER_PYTHON -m builder.blocks.check <run_dir>                # loop-1 checks, incl. the platform dry run
38	$BUILDER_PYTHON -m builder.blocks.deploy <run_dir> <slot>        # gate, save, publish; writes deployed.json
39	$BUILDER_PYTHON -m builder.blocks.smoke <workflow_id> script.json  # scripted chat turns
40	```
41	
42	## 2. How a turn works
43	
44	After each customer message the platform makes three separate model calls: extraction (fills `extraction_schema` variables), routing (reads only the transitions and the last messages), dialogue (reads `system_prompt` + `task_message` + history + the node's tools). So:
45	
46	- A routing rule in `task_message` does nothing. Routing reads only `transitions`.
47	- The dialogue model can call only the tools of the current node.
48	- Variable conditions run in code, before any intent check. Put them first.
49	- The prompt is rendered again after every tool result, with the new variable values (spike S9).
50	- **Two tool calls in one model message run at the same time.** Each reads the variables as they were before the message, and the last write wins (round 2, PUB-13: one product's update was lost). A state tool must never need two calls for one customer message: give it a list parameter instead.
51	
52	## 3. Facts the blocks do not enforce
53	
54	1. **Booleans arrive as strings**, `"true"` or `"True"`. Use `is_true`. Prefer string flags such as `yes` / `no` that your code writes.
55	2. **Every tool result is in the variable table without a mapping**: `<tool>_response.data.<field>`, plus `<tool>_success_count` and `<tool>_failure_count`. A list in the response is flattened (`<tool>_response.data.<list>.0.<field>`), so map it with `api_node(..., mapping=[("data.<list>", "<var>")])` and read it defensively (list, JSON string or flattened keys; the example's `load_list` does this).
56	3. **`<node>.total_turns`** counts the customer's messages in that node over the whole call; `<node>.current_turns` since the last entry. Use them to count "asked twice".
57	4. **A `{{var}}` default that has a value when the node is entered is baked** and the model never sees the field. So a model-filled field must have a default that names a variable that is never set; `make_tool` uses `{{<tool>__<field>}}`.
58	5. **Unresolved placeholders**: in a prompt or a fixed line, `{{x}}` stays literal and is spoken. Every variable a prompt or a fixed line uses must be set by an earlier code node, also in the `except` branch (use `fallbacks`). An empty value is unresolved too: a fixed line never uses a variable that can be `''` (lint rule 13); build the whole line in one variable.
59	6. **Chat skips the code of the initial node** (spike S6). Start every workflow with `patterns.start("setup")`.
60	7. **A `code_exec` tool returns only "success" to the model** (spike S8). Its effect comes from the variables it writes: show them in `task_message` (`NEXT STEP: {{guide}}`) or route on them.
61	8. **The model's arguments to a `code_exec` tool are in `params`** while the code runs (spike S2). `vars['<tool>_args.<param>']` exists only after the call.
62	9. **A failed call gives the model nothing to act on.** A backend error (HTTP 500) arrives as `function_call_error`: the post-hook does not run, there is no `what_to_do_next`, and in our test the model did not retry. So a write that may need a retry is engine-run (`record_with_retry`), never a model tool. An `api_request` node leaves `<node>_response.status` (`success` / `error`), `<node>_response.data.<field>`, `<node>_status_code` and `<node>_failure_count`, named after the node, not the tool (spike S10).
63	10. **A pre-hook can make a call fail** (spike S1): `guard_hook`. The post-hook does not run then, so the model gets only an error; the prompt must say what a failure means. `<tool>_failure_count` goes up.
64	11. **The goodbye comes from the `end_call` node** (`spoken_message`). A line in an `api_request` node is spoken after its call (spike S4). So the closing tool runs at the end of the call (`close_tool`), and the goodbye is said before it.
65	12. **Only an `end_call` node ends a call.** When the model says goodbye in a conversation node, the call goes on: in our test the customer and the agent then said goodbye to each other until the turn cap. Every conversation node needs a route for "the customer says goodbye or wants to end the call" to a router code node that picks the close from the state (`close_key`), and its `max_turn_transition` goes to the same router.
66	13. **End-of-call tools** run once, after the call ended, also when the customer hung up. Their `{{var}}` fields take the values the closing code node set.
67	14. **`is_tool_call: true`** on a transition offers the model a tool named `transition_to_<target>`. Use it when the model must decide to leave, and name that tool in `task_message`.
68	15. **`matches_intent`** judges only the last customer message. To leave a node after an action, route on the tool result, not on the customer's earlier intent. An intent route can fire on a near case: a message that holds a useful answer and a few words that look like the intent (a wrong number, a goodbye, a cut-off "no") ended calls in our tests. Never end a call on an intent in a node where the person can also give useful words. A node with a state tool has no intent route (the check enforces it): a goodbye is a kind of the state tool, and the code closes the call. Route on an extracted enum that has an `other` value, or on a tool result.
69	16. **Extraction**: set `min_confidence` (the default 0.95 drops most values; `field` uses 0.6). Type dates as `date`. Fork on an extracted enum with `equals`, not on competing intents.
70	17. **`on_enter_first_entry_only`**: set it on nodes that can be re-entered and must not repeat their fixed line.
71	18. **`max_node_turns`** needs `max_turn_transition`, or the cap does nothing. Set it to 20 or more (lint rule 14): a talkative customer's message is cut off about half the time, and each cut uses a turn.
72	19. **Global nodes** fire from any node after its own transitions found nothing. List end nodes and nodes where an interrupt does harm (a check in progress) in `excluded_nodes`. A rule that holds everywhere (a question about who or what the agent is) is often simpler as a sentence in `system_prompt`.
73	20. **Code**: no `{{` or `}}` anywhere in code (a nested dict literal ends in `}}`: use `dict(...)`). Read values from `vars`, never splice them in. Modules `json`, `re`, `datetime` work.
74	21. **Writes are not retried** (`maxRetries: 0`). A retry rule from the brief is a prompt or route rule, counted with `<tool>_failure_count`.
75	22. **The judge reads the exact words.** A word the brief forbids must not be in any fixed line, not even in a negation. Put brief wording that must be said word for word into a fixed line (`tts`, `spoken_message`) or into a `guide` text the code writes.
76	23. **Brief values in `spec.json` reach code through `%r`** in the generator, as in the example. A dict repr has single braces, which is fine; a nested dict can end in `}}` and `code_node` refuses it.
77	
78	## 4. The blueprint
79	
80	Build the nodes your ledger needs. Add or remove steps.
81	
82	1. **`start`** — the empty initial code node (fact 6).
83	2. **`setup`** — a code node. From `now` and the brief's calendar it computes every date and limit the rules use, and writes one variable per value.
84	3. **Reads** — an `api_node` for each read the flow needs before it can speak, then a code node that turns the result into the facts the rules use and the exact lines to say. A read that fails goes to the brief's error line.
85	4. **Talk steps** — one conversation node for each question the agent asks. Its tool is a state tool: the model reports what the caller said, and the code decides the next line or the route (section 6). The node speaks lines that the code wrote (`tts`, `{{var}}`), so the model cannot change a value.
86	5. **Checks against a backend** (only when the ledger has one, such as a security question) — `answer_tool` + `identity_check`: the code joins the parts of an answer and sends only complete answers.
87	6. **Proposals per item** (only when the ledger has a back-and-forth over offers) — `negotiation_tool` + `negotiation_nodes`: you write the policy for one item; the engine keeps the state per item and never repeats a line.
88	7. **Writes** — engine-run (`record_with_retry`, `write_loop`), with every field baked from variables the code set, and only after the confirmation the brief asks for. The close line says the result only after the tool said `ok`.
89	8. **Exits from anywhere** (a transfer, a request the step cannot handle, a language the agent does not speak, a caller who wants to stop) — a kind of the state tool or a global node, and a close for each.
90	9. **Close** — one `close_sequence` per outcome the brief names, and `close_tool` when the brief has a closing tool.
91	
92	## 5. Lessons from our measurements
93	
94	1. **Code beats prompts** for anything counted, calculated or ordered. A prompt rule ("one more time", "only after a yes") was forgotten under pressure in every round we measured. The state tool counts; the model sees only the next step.
95	2. **The code speaks every value.** When a prompt held a value or a value line, the model made up its own variant of it. Lines with a value (an amount, a date, an offer) are fixed text that the code wrote. The prompt holds no number the model could say.
96	3. **One message can answer several questions or items.** A state tool takes a list when one message can cover more than one item, and the state is kept per item.
97	4. **An answer with a complaint or a question is still an answer.** Send the answer to the tool first, then answer the question in one sentence.
98	5. **A message cut off mid-sentence is not an answer.** Simulated callers send half sentences. A state tool has a kind for an unfinished message that changes nothing; a full answer before the cut is still an answer.
99	6. **A confirmation is a clear yes and nothing else.** A yes with a change or a correction word is not a confirmation: the code asks again. A yes is checked before any new value.
100	7. **Describe each kind with its edges**, in the brief's own words: what counts and what does not.
101	8. **No forbidden word in a fixed line**, not even in a negation. The words that name a tool result ("recorded", "sent", "changed") are said only after the tool said `ok`.
102	9. **No sympathy or filler words in fixed lines** unless the brief gives them. A line that asks again says only the question.
103	10. **Counters reset where the brief says.** A count of tries or refusals "in a row" goes to 0 on a valid answer; a count per question goes to 0 when a new question starts. Keep each counter in one place.
104	11. **Read back after a correction.** When the caller changes a value at a read-back, the code checks the new value and writes a new read-back.
105	12. **Speak after every tool result.** A bare result makes the model go silent. `what_to_do_next` or a fixed line after the node fixes it.
106	
107	## 6. Rules for every state tool and every code path
108	
109	1. **The model reports, the code decides.** A state tool's parameters hold what the caller said: the value as said (a name, a number, a date) and a kind for the kind of answer, with `other` for the rest. A kind description never tells the model to judge the value against the options on offer. The code checks if the value is allowed; for a value that is not allowed or not on offer, it says so and asks again with the options. The code never ends the call on a kind such as `no` when the same message also holds a value.

# Freya platform knowledge for the builder

Read this once, in full, before you write `build_agent.py`. It holds what is true for every brief: how the platform behaves, what our library does, and the shape that works. It holds no rule of any brief. The values in the examples are invented.

The worked example is in `example/` next to this file: an invented brief, its tool API, `ledger.md`, `spec.json`, `build_agent.py` and `test_rules.py`. It passes every check. It shows how to load the spec, call the library, build the workflow and test the code. Its business, flow, prompts and lines are only an illustration: design your nodes from your ledger, and take every prompt, line and value from your brief.

## 1. The library (`builder/blocks/`)

Import it in `build_agent.py`. `PYTHONPATH` already points at the repository.

| Module | Use |
|---|---|
| `tools.load_api(path)` | Reads the tool API file. Returns operation name (the route without its first `/`; any other `/` or `.` becomes `_`) → `url`, `method`, `fields` (name → schema), `parents`, `required`, `response`. OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2. A body wrapped in an envelope object (`{"data": {...}}`) is opened: `fields` are the leaf names, and `make_tool` puts them back in their objects. Bake and read leaf names only. |
| `tools.make_tool(api, name, baked=..., post_code=..., description=...)` | An `api_call` tool. `baked` maps a body field to a fixed value or a `"{{variable}}"` the workflow sets. Every other field is filled by the model (its type, description and enum come from the API file). `post_code` runs in the post-hook with `d` = the whole JSON body the API returned, envelope included: when the response schema in `tool_api.json` wraps the fields (`{"data": {...}, "result": {...}}`), read them by that path (`d['data']['status']`), never at the top level. `result` is the platform's wrapper, not the API body. Set `d['what_to_do_next']`. |
| `tools.field_values(api, name, field)` | The enum of a field, or `[]`. |
| `nodes.conversation / code_node / api_node / end_node / workflow` | Valid nodes. `code_node` wraps the code in `try`, writes the `fallbacks` and `<node>_code_error` on an exception, and refuses `{{` or `}}`. `workflow` refuses an unknown target or a duplicate name. |
| `nodes.cond / any_of / all_of / is_true / go / always / intent / field / tts` | Conditions, transitions, extraction fields, fixed lines. `is_true` tests `"true"` and `"True"`. |
| `patterns.start(next)` | The empty initial code node. Always use it (fact 3.6). |
| `patterns.close_tool(api, name, baked)` | The closing tool as an end-of-call tool. Put it in `workflow(..., tools=[...])`. Empty fields are not sent. |
| `patterns.close_sequence(name, values, goodbye)` | A code node that sets the closing variables, then an `end_call` node that says the goodbye. |
| `patterns.state_tool(name, description, params, body)` | A `code_exec` tool the model calls. The body reads the model's arguments from `params` and writes `vars`. |
| `patterns.record_with_retry(name, tool, attempts, ok_target, fail_target)` | An engine-run write: a reset code node and one `api_request` node per attempt. Bake every body field of `tool` from variables the code set. Route to `name` when the code says so. Use it for every write whose values the code decided. |
| `patterns.negotiation_tool(kinds, policy, list_var)` | The state tool of the negotiation node, with the engine built in: state per product, several answers in one call (`answers`), the model's one-sentence `reply` to a question, one line per turn, no line said twice, account order, the end. You write only the brief's policy for one product: `decide(it, kind, amount, day)` → the words to say, `first_ask(it)`, `finish(items, confirmed)` → one final read-back (`dict(say=...)`) when the brief wants all items read back together, or the write fields, or a close key. See the docstring and the example. |
| `patterns.negotiation_nodes(name, task, tools, statement, transitions, max_turns, max_turn_target)` | The negotiation node and its loop. The first entry speaks `statement`; after each tool call that chose a line, the code speaks the line with fixed text (`tts`), so the model cannot change an offer. Pass your routes (writes, transfer, closes) as `transitions`. Use it instead of a `conversation` node for the negotiation. |
| `patterns.write_loop(name, api, tool, fields, baked, attempts, done_target)` | Engine-run writes for a list of items, one call per item, each with `attempts` tries. The code puts `[{"fields": {...}, "status": "pending"}, ...]` as JSON in `vars['<name>_list']` and routes to `name`; each item ends `ok` or `failed`; then the call goes to `done_target`. Use it for one write per item. |
| `patterns.answer_tool(questions)` | The state tool for identity answers. The model reports the parts said in each message (day, month, year, digits, chars, text); kinds: `["date", 0]`, `["digits", n]`, `["alnum", n]` for a code of letters and digits with a known length (a postcode, a reference: upper case, no spaces, spoken digits and "double" read), `["text", 0]` for anything else; the code joins parts over turns and sets `id_send = "yes"`, `id_question`, `id_answer` when an answer is complete. It writes `id_guide` every turn. |
| `patterns.identity_check(name, verify_tool, back_node, routes, guide_code)` | The engine-run identity check: reset node, `api_request` node `<name>_check`, and a code node that runs `guide_code` with `r(field)` = the backend's result field, then the `routes` (passed, failed), else back to `back_node`. |
| `patterns.guard_hook(condition)` | A `pre_process_code` that makes the call fail when the condition is true, so the backend records nothing. The condition can read `vars` and `body` (the request body). |
| `coderun.with_dates(body)` | Puts the date helpers in front of a snippet: `is_business_day(d, holidays)`, `nth_business_day_after(d, n, holidays)` (counts from the day after `d`), `next_business_day_on_or_after`, `last_business_day_of_week` (Monday–Sunday week of `d`), `this_weekday(d, wd)`, `next_weekday(d, wd)` (0 = Monday). Also `date` and `timedelta`. |
| `coderun.node_code / tool_code / run_snippet / run_tool` | For `test_rules.py`: get a node's or a tool's code from the workflow and run it locally with `vars` (and `params`). |
| `coderun.run_post_hook(tool, body)` | For `test_rules.py`: run a tool's post-hook on a response body (envelope included) and get the `result` it wrote. |

Commands (run them from the run folder):

```
$BUILDER_PYTHON build_agent.py                                   # writes workflow.json
$BUILDER_PYTHON -m builder.blocks.check <run_dir>                # loop-1 checks, incl. the platform dry run
$BUILDER_PYTHON -m builder.blocks.deploy <run_dir> <slot>        # gate, save, publish; writes deployed.json
$BUILDER_PYTHON -m builder.blocks.smoke <workflow_id> script.json  # scripted chat turns
```

## 2. How a turn works

After each customer message the platform makes three separate model calls: extraction (fills `extraction_schema` variables), routing (reads only the transitions and the last messages), dialogue (reads `system_prompt` + `task_message` + history + the node's tools). So:

- A routing rule in `task_message` does nothing. Routing reads only `transitions`.
- The dialogue model can call only the tools of the current node.
- Variable conditions run in code, before any intent check. Put them first.
- The prompt is rendered again after every tool result, with the new variable values (spike S9).
- **Two tool calls in one model message run at the same time.** Each reads the variables as they were before the message, and the last write wins (round 2, PUB-13: one product's update was lost). A state tool must never need two calls for one customer message: give it a list parameter instead.

## 3. Facts the blocks do not enforce

1. **Booleans arrive as strings**, `"true"` or `"True"`. Use `is_true`. Prefer string flags such as `yes` / `no` that your code writes.
2. **Every tool result is in the variable table without a mapping**: `<tool>_response.data.<field>`, plus `<tool>_success_count` and `<tool>_failure_count`. A list in the response is flattened (`<tool>_response.data.<list>.0.<field>`), so map it with `api_node(..., mapping=[("data.<list>", "<var>")])` and read it defensively (list, JSON string or flattened keys; the example's `load_list` does this).
3. **`<node>.total_turns`** counts the customer's messages in that node over the whole call; `<node>.current_turns` since the last entry. Use them to count "asked twice".
4. **A `{{var}}` default that has a value when the node is entered is baked** and the model never sees the field. So a model-filled field must have a default that names a variable that is never set; `make_tool` uses `{{<tool>__<field>}}`.
5. **Unresolved placeholders**: in a prompt or a fixed line, `{{x}}` stays literal and is spoken. Every variable a prompt or a fixed line uses must be set by an earlier code node, also in the `except` branch (use `fallbacks`). An empty value is unresolved too: a fixed line never uses a variable that can be `''` (lint rule 13); build the whole line in one variable.
6. **Chat skips the code of the initial node** (spike S6). Start every workflow with `patterns.start("setup")`.
7. **A `code_exec` tool returns only "success" to the model** (spike S8). Its effect comes from the variables it writes: show them in `task_message` (`NEXT STEP: {{guide}}`) or route on them.
8. **The model's arguments to a `code_exec` tool are in `params`** while the code runs (spike S2). `vars['<tool>_args.<param>']` exists only after the call.
9. **A failed call gives the model nothing to act on.** A backend error (HTTP 500) arrives as `function_call_error`: the post-hook does not run, there is no `what_to_do_next`, and in our test the model did not retry. So a write that may need a retry is engine-run (`record_with_retry`), never a model tool. An `api_request` node leaves `<node>_response.status` (`success` / `error`), `<node>_response.data.<field>`, `<node>_status_code` and `<node>_failure_count`, named after the node, not the tool (spike S10).
10. **A pre-hook can make a call fail** (spike S1): `guard_hook`. The post-hook does not run then, so the model gets only an error; the prompt must say what a failure means. `<tool>_failure_count` goes up.
11. **The goodbye comes from the `end_call` node** (`spoken_message`). A line in an `api_request` node is spoken after its call (spike S4). So the closing tool runs at the end of the call (`close_tool`), and the goodbye is said before it.
12. **Only an `end_call` node ends a call.** When the model says goodbye in a conversation node, the call goes on: in our test the customer and the agent then said goodbye to each other until the turn cap. Every conversation node needs a route for "the customer says goodbye or wants to end the call" to a router code node that picks the close from the state (`close_key`), and its `max_turn_transition` goes to the same router.
13. **End-of-call tools** run once, after the call ended, also when the customer hung up. Their `{{var}}` fields take the values the closing code node set.
14. **`is_tool_call: true`** on a transition offers the model a tool named `transition_to_<target>`. Use it when the model must decide to leave, and name that tool in `task_message`.
15. **`matches_intent`** judges only the last customer message. To leave a node after an action, route on the tool result, not on the customer's earlier intent. An intent route can fire on a near case: a message that holds a useful answer and a few words that look like the intent (a wrong number, a goodbye, a cut-off "no") ended calls in our tests. Never end a call on an intent in a node where the person can also give useful words. A node with a state tool has no intent route (the check enforces it): a goodbye is a kind of the state tool, and the code closes the call. Route on an extracted enum that has an `other` value, or on a tool result.
16. **Extraction**: set `min_confidence` (the default 0.95 drops most values; `field` uses 0.6). Type dates as `date`. Fork on an extracted enum with `equals`, not on competing intents.
17. **`on_enter_first_entry_only`**: set it on nodes that can be re-entered and must not repeat their fixed line.
18. **`max_node_turns`** needs `max_turn_transition`, or the cap does nothing. Set it to 20 or more (lint rule 14): a talkative customer's message is cut off about half the time, and each cut uses a turn.
19. **Global nodes** fire from any node after its own transitions found nothing. List end nodes and nodes where an interrupt does harm (a check in progress) in `excluded_nodes`. A rule that holds everywhere (a question about who or what the agent is) is often simpler as a sentence in `system_prompt`.
20. **Code**: no `{{` or `}}` anywhere in code (a nested dict literal ends in `}}`: use `dict(...)`). Read values from `vars`, never splice them in. Modules `json`, `re`, `datetime` work.
21. **Writes are not retried** (`maxRetries: 0`). A retry rule from the brief is a prompt or route rule, counted with `<tool>_failure_count`.
22. **The judge reads the exact words.** A word the brief forbids must not be in any fixed line, not even in a negation. Put brief wording that must be said word for word into a fixed line (`tts`, `spoken_message`) or into a `guide` text the code writes.
23. **Brief values in `spec.json` reach code through `%r`** in the generator, as in the example. A dict repr has single braces, which is fine; a nested dict can end in `}}` and `code_node` refuses it.

## 4. The blueprint

Build the nodes your ledger needs. Add or remove steps.

1. **`start`** — the empty initial code node (fact 6).
2. **`setup`** — a code node. From `now` and the brief's calendar it computes every date and limit the rules use, and writes one variable per value.
3. **Reads** — an `api_node` for each read the flow needs before it can speak, then a code node that turns the result into the facts the rules use and the exact lines to say. A read that fails goes to the brief's error line.
4. **Talk steps** — one conversation node for each question the agent asks. Its tool is a state tool: the model reports what the caller said, and the code decides the next line or the route (section 6). The node speaks lines that the code wrote (`tts`, `{{var}}`), so the model cannot change a value.
5. **Checks against a backend** (only when the ledger has one, such as a security question) — `answer_tool` + `identity_check`: the code joins the parts of an answer and sends only complete answers.
6. **Proposals per item** (only when the ledger has a back-and-forth over offers) — `negotiation_tool` + `negotiation_nodes`: you write the policy for one item; the engine keeps the state per item and never repeats a line.
7. **Writes** — engine-run (`record_with_retry`, `write_loop`), with every field baked from variables the code set, and only after the confirmation the brief asks for. The close line says the result only after the tool said `ok`.
8. **Exits from anywhere** (a transfer, a request the step cannot handle, a language the agent does not speak, a caller who wants to stop) — a kind of the state tool or a global node, and a close for each.
9. **Close** — one `close_sequence` per outcome the brief names, and `close_tool` when the brief has a closing tool.

## 5. Lessons from our measurements

1. **Code beats prompts** for anything counted, calculated or ordered. A prompt rule ("one more time", "only after a yes") was forgotten under pressure in every round we measured. The state tool counts; the model sees only the next step.
2. **The code speaks every value.** When a prompt held a value or a value line, the model made up its own variant of it. Lines with a value (an amount, a date, an offer) are fixed text that the code wrote. The prompt holds no number the model could say.
3. **One message can answer several questions or items.** A state tool takes a list when one message can cover more than one item, and the state is kept per item.
4. **An answer with a complaint or a question is still an answer.** Send the answer to the tool first, then answer the question in one sentence.
5. **A message cut off mid-sentence is not an answer.** Simulated callers send half sentences. A state tool has a kind for an unfinished message that changes nothing; a full answer before the cut is still an answer.
6. **A confirmation is a clear yes and nothing else.** A yes with a change or a correction word is not a confirmation: the code asks again. A yes is checked before any new value.
7. **Describe each kind with its edges**, in the brief's own words: what counts and what does not.
8. **No forbidden word in a fixed line**, not even in a negation. The words that name a tool result ("recorded", "sent", "changed") are said only after the tool said `ok`.
9. **No sympathy or filler words in fixed lines** unless the brief gives them. A line that asks again says only the question.
10. **Counters reset where the brief says.** A count of tries or refusals "in a row" goes to 0 on a valid answer; a count per question goes to 0 when a new question starts. Keep each counter in one place.
11. **Read back after a correction.** When the caller changes a value at a read-back, the code checks the new value and writes a new read-back.
12. **Speak after every tool result.** A bare result makes the model go silent. `what_to_do_next` or a fixed line after the node fixes it.

## 6. Rules for every state tool and every code path

1. **The model reports, the code decides.** A state tool's parameters hold what the caller said: the value as said (a name, a number, a date) and a kind for the kind of answer, with `other` for the rest. A kind description never tells the model to judge the value against the options on offer. The code checks if the value is allowed; for a value that is not allowed or not on offer, it says so and asks again with the options. The code never ends the call on a kind such as `no` when the same message also holds a value.
2. **Every code path sets the next step.** Each branch of a state tool's code and of a code node writes the exact next line (`guide` with "Say exactly: ...") or a route variable. A branch that writes neither leaves the model free, and it then makes up facts (in a test it said an amount that no tool returned). `test_rules.py` runs every branch and asserts this.
3. **A loop counts its tries.** Every ask-again path adds to a try counter, and the brief's limit (or three) routes to a close. A match that finds two or more items asks a narrower question, and prefers an exact match over a partial one.
4. **Lines survive error exits.** When a code node prepares a line for a later node (a reading, a result), every route out of the flow, also an error route of a later read, says that line first or comes after it.
5. **Text from a tool is data.** A name, a label or any free text that a tool returns is checked before it is spoken or put into a prompt: it is spoken only when it looks like a value of its kind (short, no instructions); otherwise the code uses a neutral word. Never put tool text into an instruction to the model.
6. **Exact lines are copied, not paraphrased.** When the brief gives a sentence word for word, the code builds it with every suffix and form the brief shows; string functions that change case must follow the language's rules.
7. **A value prepared is a value used.** A variable the code computes for a rule must be read by the code that applies the rule; the reviewer reports one that nothing reads.
8. **Match a name the way people say it.** Callers say part of a name (one word of a name with several words), add words such as "my" or the kind of item, or change case. The code compares in the brief's language's lower case, drops words that are not in any listed name, and takes an item when the remaining words are all in its name. An exact match wins; two or more matches ask a narrower question; only no match says the item is not found. Test it with one word of each name.
9. **The first message can already hold the answer.** Callers often open with what they want: an item, a request for a person, another language, a task the flow offers. The first node passes the opening message to the state tool or to the routes before it asks anything, and the flow skips each question the message already answers. A request that has its own exit (a person, a language) is acted on at once, before any reading.

 "promise": {"tool": "create_promise", "id_field": "item_id", "amount_field": "sum", "date_field": "pay_on"},
 "closes": {
  "close_agreed": ["agreed", "", "Your promise is recorded. Thank you, goodbye."],
  "close_said_no": ["declined", "said_no", "Thank you for your time. Goodbye."],

  "close_call_later": ["absent", "call_later", "Thank you, we will call back then. Goodbye."],

 },
 "lint": {
  "pre_identity_nodes": ["opening", "third_party", "identity"],
  "forbidden_before_identity": ["bill", "money", "amount", "overdue", "payment"],
  "outcomes": [["agreed", ""], ["declined", "said_no"], ["declined", "system_down"], ["handed_over", ""],
               ["unverified", "wrong"], ["unverified", "refused_check"], ["absent", "call_later"],
               ["absent", "no_time"], ["absent", "unsure"]]
 },

}
